Respiratory metabolism was evaluated in adult Common smoky honeyeaters under standard thermoneutral conditions. The highest basal oxygen consumption recorded from individuals at rest reached 122 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 122 milliliters of oxygen per hour], measured at a core body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value characteristic of a moderately active passerine of its body size. Newly hatched nestlings were found to weigh approximately 6.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.1 grams] upon emergence from the egg, a modest initial mass that underscores the altricial developmental mode typical of meliphagids. Growth proceeds rapidly under sustained parental provisioning, with downy chicks gaining mass steadily during the first weeks of brooding. The combination of a relatively elevated metabolic rate and a small starting mass necessitates frequent feeding visits by both adults to sustain the nestling's thermal homeostasis and tissue accretion, particularly during the cooler montane mornings where these birds are most commonly encountered.

Data on reproductive output in Melipotes fumigatus are limited, but extrapolations from the closely related Acanthagenys rufogularis provide useful comparative benchmarks. This relatively short nestling phase allows broods to fledge before the onset of the harsher montane weather patterns that characterize the higher elevations these birds inhabit. After leaving the nest, the developing chick continues to receive parental attention for several additional weeks before achieving full foraging independence.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, with females attaining a smaller ultimate size than males. The maximum wet weight recorded for adult females is 48 grams [Wwi = 48 grams], a value at the lower end of the reported range from 42 to 54 grams. Males, in contrast, achieve a heavier asymptotic mass of 53 grams [Wwi = 53 grams], with field measurements spanning 46 to 60 grams. This size difference is consistent with the pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism seen in some meliphagids, though the ecological drivers remain unclear. The larger body mass of males may confer advantages in territorial defense over nectar resources, which are often patchily distributed across their subalpine habitat. These mass values place Melipotes fumigatus in the mid-range of body sizes for the genus, comparable in stature to other highland honeyeaters of New Guinea.

Longevity data for wild Common smoky honeyeaters are scarce, but extrapolations from mark-recapture studies and captive records suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 12.5 years [am = approximately 12.5 years] under favorable conditions at a core body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The first successful breeding event is deferred until roughly 1.7 years since birth [tR = roughly 1.7 years since birth] at the same temperature, representing a significant delay relative to smaller-bodied passerines. This combination of moderate longevity and delayed reproduction is characteristic of montane bird species, which often experience reduced predation pressure but face energetic constraints imposed by cool, seasonal environments. The overall life-history strategy appears geared toward adult survival and repeated breeding attempts across several seasons, rather than a single intense reproductive burst. Such a pace-of-life syndrome aligns well with the stable, resource-limited conditions typical of tropical highland ecosystems.
